Les LLMs écrivent du code, des tests, de la documentation, des synthèses, et ils le font à une vitesse qui était inimaginable il y a peu. Je les utilise, et vous aussi probablement. Mais plus je les pratique, plus un constat s’impose : ils excellent à produire du plausible. Ils recombinent, reformulent, complètent ce qui existe déjà. items.title: A team of AI agents needs Scrum, not a better model
items.excerpt: "Agent = Model + Harness" describes one AI agent well and a team of agents badly. Once agents work together, the defects that matter come from handoffs, shared records and two agents doing the same work. A better model fixes none of those. A team needs a second line: Team = Agents + Coordination. Scrum already supplies the coordination. My own team of AI agents runs on Scrum, and its records show where the defects come from. items.title: The Framework is Not the Point
items.excerpt: Image I am not sure how many times I have explained to my kids that no, they probably won't use Calculus. And maybe they won't need to know the details of Earth Science. Or how Pride and Prejudice ends. But that's not the point. The point of going to High School is to learn how to learn. How to assimilate and analyze data. To find out what you're capable of and to give you confidence that yes, you can do that thing - whatever "that thing" is for you. Scrum has something in common with Calculus, it turns out. items.title: When AI Speeds Up Implementation, Test Your Ideas with Small Experiments
items.excerpt: When AI makes implementation faster, it can be tempting to start the next feature too. But we need to make sure we are not adding unnecessary features. Before asking how to reduce the wait for review and validation, we need to look at how long it takes to get feedback from customers and users. Shorten lead time so that you can get feedback on what you have built sooner. To do that, reduce batch size: the amount of work you take on as a single unit.
